payload.dispatch: The black core of a pencil is graphite, not lead, and has never contained the element lead. A large deposit of graphite was discovered at Borrowdale in Cumbria, England, in 1765. In 1795 Nicolas-Jacques Conté found a way to mix powdered graphite with clay and fire the rods in a kiln, and on 30 March 1858 Hymen Lipman received the first patent for attaching an eraser to the end of a pencil.

evidence.title: Borrowdale
evidence.text: In 1565 (some sources say as early as 1500), a large deposit of graphite was discovered on the approach to Grey Knotts from the hamlet of Seathwaite in Borrowdale parish, Cumbria, England.

evidence.title: Clay, kilns and erasers
evidence.text: In 1795, Nicolas-Jacques Conté discovered a method of mixing powdered graphite with clay and forming the mixture into rods that were then fired in a kiln. On 30 March 1858, Hymen Lipman received the first patent for attaching an eraser to the end of a pencil.

reveal.explanation: The Borrowdale graphite was found in 1565, two centuries before the dispatch's date. Conté's clay process of 1795 and Lipman's eraser patent of 30 March 1858 are correct.

sources.excerpt: The black core of pencils is still referred to as lead, even though it never contained the element lead. In 1565 (some sources say as early as 1500), a large deposit of graphite was discovered on the approach to Grey Knotts from the hamlet of Seathwaite in Borrowdale parish, Cumbria, England. In 1795, Nicolas-Jacques Conté discovered a method of mixing powdered graphite with clay and forming the mixture into rods that were then fired in a kiln. On 30 March 1858, Hymen Lipman received the first patent for attaching an eraser to the end of a pencil.
